outsideCityLimits.value: Outside city limits, the Texas law that lets counties set building standards for houses is narrow. It applies only where a county has opted in, and only to a new house or a big addition started after September 1, 2009. That law doesn’t require county approval before building starts, and the builder hires the inspectors (a licensed engineer, architect or state-licensed inspector, among others). So the paperwork for a house here may be the builder’s inspection reports, not a county permit. Ask the seller for them, and ask the county what it has on file for the address.
outsideCityLimits.note: Texas Local Government Code ch. 233, subchapter F.

outsideCityJobs.value: Outside city limits, the Texas law on county building standards covers only new houses and additions that grow a house by more than half. So ask the county whether the {work} needed a permit here, and ask the seller for the contractor’s invoice.

nearCityLimits.value: Near a city? Where a city has adopted a building code for the area just outside its limits (its extraterritorial jurisdiction), the city’s code applies there instead. If the house is close to a city, ask that city too.

olderRecordsLaw.value: Under the Texas Public Information Act (Government Code chapter 552), anyone can ask a Texas city or county for its records, unless a law makes them confidential. The office has to produce them promptly. If it can’t within 10 business days, it has to tell you in writing when they’ll be ready.
